1.5c Hunter’s Late Afternoon.title: 1.5c Hunter’s Late Afternoon
1.5c Hunter’s Late Afternoon.text:
When you open the door, Tomas stands on the threshold, his face drawn with worry. The cooper's usual steadiness has deserted him. His cap is crooked, and his hands are red from the cold.
“Elara, I need your help,” he says. “We've got a deer in the yard. Found it caught in the boundary fence. It's dead, or near enough, and if we leave it until morning, the meat will be spoiled.”
You reach for your outer cloak.
“Where?”
“Behind the old storehouse. It must have come down from the northern woods.”
You pause at that.
The northern woods are where the strange sound came from earlier. You have tried not to think about it since, but the memory has stayed with you: that deep, unnatural note travelling through the earth, followed by a silence that seemed to swallow every living thing around it.
“Did you see anything else?” you ask.
Tomas shakes his head. “Only the deer. Will you come?”
“Of course.”
You collect your knife, a length of clean cord, and a canvas sheet. Kael rises from beside the hearth, already reaching for his cloak.
“I'll come too.”
“You can stay here.”
“And let you drag a deer through the mud by yourself?”
“I've done it before.”
“Yes. And complained about your back for three days afterwards.”
You give him a flat look. He answers with the familiar, infuriating half-smile that has accompanied so many of your arguments over the years.
“Bring the lantern,” you say at last.
Outside, the cold has sharpened. The lane is slick beneath your boots, and the evening mist gathers low around the fences. Tomas leads you past the last cottages towards the storehouse, where the ground slopes gently towards the forest boundary.
The deer lies on its side beside a broken section of fence.
It is a young stag, its coat dark with moisture. One hind leg is tangled in the splintered wood, but there is little blood. You kneel beside it, examining the wound and the position of its limbs. The injury should have been survivable, had it been found sooner.
“Poor thing,” Tomas mutters.
You reach to inspect the animal's neck.
The fur beneath your fingertips is strangely warm.
Not the lingering warmth of a recently dead body. This feels different, concentrated beneath the skin, as though heat has been trapped deep inside the flesh. You draw your hand back and rub your fingers together.
A faint grey residue clings to your palm.
Ash.
You look at the stag again. Its coat is wet with mist, but the grey dust beneath your hand is dry and fine, settling into the creases of your skin.
“Kael.”
He crouches beside you, holding the lantern closer.
For a moment, neither of you speaks.
Then the stag's body gives a single, small twitch.
You recoil, reaching instinctively for your knife. Tomas stumbles backwards with a startled curse.
The animal does not move again.
You wait, watching its flank. No breath comes. Its eyes remain dull and open, reflecting the lantern light.
“Muscle spasm,” you say, though you have never seen one quite like that.
Kael studies the animal's legs. “Perhaps.”
His tone suggests he does not believe it any more than you do.
You turn your attention to the ground. The mud around the stag is marked with hoofprints, deep and sharply defined. You follow them back towards the trees, expecting to find a trail leading from the forest to the broken fence.
Instead, the tracks end several paces away.
They do not fade. They do not turn aside or disappear beneath fallen leaves. They simply stop, each impression complete and clear in the mud, as though the animal had stepped out of the earth and into the air.
You stand slowly.
“Have you ever seen anything like this?” you ask.
Tomas peers over your shoulder. His face has gone pale beneath the lantern glow.
“No.”
A sound comes from the trees.
A single branch snapping under weight.
Kael lifts the lantern. You draw your knife and stare into the darkness between the trunks. The forest gives nothing back. No movement, no rustling leaves, not even the distant call of an owl.
Then, far beneath the ordinary sounds of the village, you feel a faint pulse through the soles of your boots.
Once.
A second time.
The earth seems to tighten beneath you, as if something vast has shifted in its sleep.
The lantern flame narrows to a thin blue-white point.
For one heartbeat, the ash on your fingers glows with a colourless light.
You close your hand instinctively. When you open it again, the glow is gone. The residue has crumbled into ordinary grey dust.
Behind you, Tomas whispers a prayer.
Kael steps closer, his shoulder brushing yours. He does not tell you that you imagined it. He does not ask you to explain.
“Let's get the deer back,” he says quietly.
You nod.
The work is practical and unpleasant. You free the stag's leg from the broken fence, inspect the wound once more, and secure the animal to the canvas sheet. Between you and Kael, you manage to drag it towards the village, with Tomas carrying the lantern ahead.
You keep your eyes on the path.
You do not look back towards the trees until you reach the first cottage.
When you do, the ground behind you is marked with your own footprints and the shallow drag of the canvas. Beside them, fresh hoofprints have appeared in the damp earth.
They run parallel to your trail.
They begin at the forest boundary and follow you towards the village.
There are no tracks leading away.
Kael sees them at the same moment you do. His hand closes around your forearm, steady and warm through your sleeve.
Neither of you speaks until the cottage lights surround you and the forest disappears behind the rooftops.
The deer will provide food for the village. The fence can be mended. Your knife can be cleaned, your hands washed, your work finished before the night grows any colder.
You understand all those things.
What you cannot understand is why the ash felt warm, why the earth pulsed beneath your feet, or why something has apparently followed you home without leaving a single track in the direction it came from.
Kael walks beside you, his hand lingering at your arm for a moment longer than necessary.
The village bells begin to sound the evening hour.
For the first time in your life, you find yourself wondering whether the forest has been watching you for far longer than you have been watching it.

1.6 Second Home LI Interaction.title: 1.6 Second Home LI Interaction
1.6 Second Home LI Interaction.text:
The heavy oak door closes behind you, shutting out the cold.

For a moment, you remain with your hand on the latch, listening to the wind scrape along the cottage walls. The evening's chill clings to your clothes, and your fingers ache with the cold. Beyond the shutters, the village has settled into darkness, its scattered lights blurred by the mist gathering over the lanes.

Inside, the hearth is still glowing.

Deep red embers pulse beneath the blackened logs, casting moving shadows across the stone floor and the exposed timber beams overhead. The kettle hums softly above the fire. The air smells of burning oak, fresh bread, and the dried herbs hanging in bundles near the kitchen window.

It is an ordinary evening. Your home is warm. Your tools are where you left them. Nothing has changed within these walls.

And yet the memory of the evening follows you inside.

You set down your belongings and begin removing your coat.

“You look as though you've been arguing with the weather,” Kael says.

He is sitting on the low stool beside the hearth, one boot stretched towards the warmth. He must have returned ahead of you, or perhaps he never truly left the cottage in the first place. His cloak hangs from its usual peg, and a mug rests between his hands.

“I won,” you reply.

“Of course. The weather is probably still outside, wondering what happened.”

You give him a tired look.

He holds out the second mug.

“Drink this before you decide to fight anything else.”

You take it. The herbal broth is hot enough to warm your palms through the clay, its faint bitterness softened by a little honey. You hadn't realised how cold you had become until the warmth begins to seep back into your fingers.

Kael watches you take the first sip.

“Better?”

“Marginally.”

“High praise.”

You settle beside him, close enough to share the fire's warmth. For a while, neither of you speaks. The kettle murmurs overhead, and the logs shift with a soft crackle. Outside, the wind presses against the shutters without finding a way in.

It is the sort of silence you have shared a hundred times.

You remember another winter evening, years ago, when the two of you had been caught beyond the river during a sudden snowfall. You had insisted you knew the way back. Kael had insisted you were walking in circles. Both of you had been too stubborn to admit you were lost until the river stone appeared for the third time.

“You remember that winter?” you ask.

Kael turns his head. “Which winter?”

“The one when we got lost near the river.”

“Oh, that winter.”

“You said you knew the way.”

“I did know the way.”

“We walked past the same stone three times.”

“It was a very large stone.”

“You blamed the snow.”

“The snow was clearly working against us.”

You laugh into your mug, nearly spilling the broth.

Kael grins. For a moment, the years between that frozen riverbank and this warm cottage seem to collapse. You can almost feel the snow soaking through your boots again, hear the two of you arguing while your fingers went numb, remember how he finally took your hand and pulled you towards the distant lights of the village.

You had been furious with him for laughing.

You had also refused to let go until you reached the first house.

“Your mother gave us both a lecture,” he says.

“She gave you a lecture. I was the innocent victim.”

“You convinced me to leave the path.”

“You followed me.”

“Because you looked so certain.”

You glance at him over the rim of your mug. “You have always had questionable judgement.”

“And yet I keep coming back.”

The words are spoken lightly, almost carelessly, but something about them settles between you.

Kael looks back towards the fire.

You take another sip of broth, letting the warmth spread through you. It would be easy to remain here indefinitely, trading old stories until the evening's unease becomes nothing more than a strange incident to discuss over breakfast. There is comfort in the familiar shape of your lives, in the certainty that tomorrow will bring ordinary tasks and ordinary troubles.

But you cannot quite forget the sound beneath the village.

Nor the strange light.

For a while, Kael seems content to leave those things unspoken. He reaches for a small plate on the table and offers you a baked apple wrapped in linen, its skin wrinkled from the heat.

“Where did this come from?”

“Your kitchen.”

“I know where my kitchen is.”

“Then the mystery is solved.”

You accept the apple. It is soft and sweet, fragrant with cinnamon and a little dried fruit. You eat slowly, watching the firelight shift over Kael's face.

Eventually, his smile fades.

“I've known every path in this valley since we were kids,” he says. “Every shortcut, every old boundary marker, every place the ground turns treacherous after rain. I could walk from here to the river in the dark and tell you where I was by the sound of the water.”

He pauses, turning his mug between his hands.

“But tonight, the whole place feels different. Like something is waiting just outside the fence.”

The words settle into the quiet.

You glance towards the window. The shutters are closed, but you find yourself imagining the darkness beyond them: the empty lane, the gardens, the fields, and the forest rising beyond the far boundary.

“Perhaps we are simply tired,” you say.

“Perhaps.”

He doesn't sound convinced.

“People have lived here for generations,” you continue. “The village has survived bad winters, poor harvests, sickness, and worse things than a strange noise in the woods.”

“I know.”

“Then why are you looking at me as though you expect me to have an answer?”

Kael's expression softens.

“Because when something is wrong, you're usually the first person I want to tell.”

You lower your mug.

He looks at you directly now, without the teasing smile or the easy deflection. There is no demand in his expression, no expectation that you will make sense of the evening or reassure him that everything is fine.

Only honesty.

“I don't know what happened out there,” he says. “I don't know whether it means anything. But I know you felt it too.”

You did.

And perhaps that is what frightens you most: not the strange light or the impossible sounds, but the fact that someone else saw enough to believe you.

The fire shifts, sending a brief shower of sparks up the chimney.

Kael's hand rests on the stone between you. Close enough to touch. Not quite touching yours.

What happens next depends, perhaps, on what the two of you have been to each other lately.

You nudge his boot with yours.

“You're becoming gloomy in your old age.”

Kael raises an eyebrow. “I'm younger than you.”

“By a few months.”

“Enough to make your accusation deeply insulting.”

“I'm sorry. I didn't realise you were so sensitive.”

He reaches for the last piece of apple, and you catch his wrist before he can take it.

“That's mine.”

“You've had most of it.”

“And now I'm protecting what's left.”

His laughter comes easily, and yours follows. The room feels warmer for it. Whatever else has changed tonight, the familiar rhythm between you remains: the teasing, the small acts of care, the comfortable knowledge that neither of you needs to perform for the other.

For a little while longer, you sit together beside the fire.

The broth cools in your hands. The wind moves over the roof. Beyond the cottage, the village rests beneath a darkening sky, and somewhere beyond the fields the forest keeps its silence.

Kael drains the last of his broth and rises, collecting the empty mugs. He pauses beside the door, wrapping his wool cloak tightly around his shoulders before giving you one final look.

“Try to get some sleep,” he says. “Tomorrow might make more sense.”

“You always were an optimist.”

His familiar half-smile returns. Then he steps into the freezing night, and you hear his boots recede along the lane. The heavy wooden latch settles into place behind him.

The cottage seems larger without him.

You stand for a while beside the hearth, watching the embers sink from orange to deep red. One by one, you extinguish the tallow candles, leaving only the fire's fading glow. You bank the remaining embers beneath a layer of ash, check the shutters, and make certain the door is secured.

The ordinary rituals steady you. There is comfort in knowing what must be done, in the familiar weight of each small responsibility.

At last, you crawl beneath the heavy wool blankets and draw them up to your chin. The cottage creaks softly around you, settling into the cold.

Your eyes grow heavy.

Somewhere beyond the village, beyond the fields and the dark boundary of the trees, the night waits.

You close your eyes, hovering at the quiet threshold of sleep.

text.content:
The village is quiet.

Not silent. It never truly becomes silent. There is always the faint complaint of timber settling in its frame, the whisper of wind slipping beneath a door, or the distant bark of a dog disturbed by something moving beyond its master's fence. Somewhere, a shutter knocks twice before falling still. A few houses away, someone coughs behind a closed window.

These are ordinary sounds. Familiar ones. The sounds of people preparing to sleep, trusting that tomorrow will arrive much as today did.

You find yourself listening to them.

The cottage has grown cold around the edges. The fire burns low in the hearth, its light reaching only as far as the nearest chair and the worn rug beneath your feet. Beyond that, the room dissolves into shadow. Your belongings sit where you left them. The wooden table bears the small knife mark you made years ago, when you were too young to understand why your mother was so cross about carelessness. A chipped cup rests beside the washbasin. Your cloak hangs from its peg, still carrying the smell of damp wool and the outdoors.

Nothing here has changed.

You move through the familiar business of closing the day. You check the latch, settle the shutters against the wind, and put away the things you will need in the morning. The gestures require little thought. Your hands know what to do even while your mind returns to the strange moments that have punctuated the afternoon and evening.

Perhaps there is a sensible explanation for each of them.

A child's fever can make her speak nonsense. Iron sometimes sings when struck at the right angle. Animals behave strangely when frightened or injured. Forests grow quiet before a change in the weather.

You have heard these explanations all your life. You have offered some of them yourself.

And yet, when you remember the pale flash at the hearth, the strange stillness of the woods, or the way the ground seemed to shiver beneath your feet, the explanations feel like stones laid over a hole in the earth. They conceal what lies beneath without making it disappear.

Outside, the wind moves along the lane.

You approach the window and lift the edge of the curtain. The village lies beneath a low ceiling of cloud. A thin line of smoke rises from the baker's chimney, though Mara's oven should have been cold for hours. Across the green, a lamp burns behind the curtains of the meeting house. Beyond the last cottages, the fields descend towards the dark line of the forest.

You know that view as well as you know your own hands.

You know where the path grows muddy after rain, where the old stone wall crumbles beside the northern field, and where the stream narrows enough to cross without wetting your boots. You know which houses shelter quarrels and which welcome unexpected visitors. You know the people who will wake before dawn and those who will sleep until the church bell reminds them of the hour.

You know what tomorrow is supposed to look like.

A small movement catches your eye.

At the far end of the lane, near the place where the cottages give way to open fields, a light appears between two houses. It is no brighter than a candle seen through a distant window. It flickers once, then again, a pale point against the dark.

You blink.

The light is gone.

For a moment, you continue staring at the empty space. Perhaps someone has closed a shutter. Perhaps a lantern has been carried indoors. There are a dozen ordinary explanations, and none requires you to stand at the window in the cold.

You let the curtain fall.

The cottage seems warmer when you turn away, though the fire has scarcely changed. You crouch beside the hearth and settle another piece of wood across the embers. A few sparks rise, twisting briefly in the air before vanishing.

One of them burns strangely pale.

Not white, exactly. More the colour of old bone beneath dust.

It lasts for less than a heartbeat. Then the wood catches, the flame turns gold, and the hearth returns to its familiar crackle.

You sit back on your heels.

The house is quiet again.

There is comfort in that. In the weight of the stone walls, in the smell of woodsmoke, in the knowledge that the door is barred and the bed is waiting. Whatever oddities the day has brought, they remain outside the boundaries of your ordinary life. You can leave them there until morning.

For now, there is nothing more to do.

You extinguish the last candle and allow the darkness to gather around you.

Before you settle for the night, you remember the warmth of Kael's presence beside the hearth: the ease with which he made room for you, the familiar sound of his voice, and the quiet certainty that you did not have to explain every silence between you.

You find yourself wishing he had stayed a little longer.

It is a small, private thought, and you let it remain so. Whatever the two of you are becoming, there will be time enough to understand it. There has always been tomorrow.

You hold on to that certainty as you prepare for bed.

You draw the blankets up to your chin and listen to the cottage settling around you. The wind brushes the shutters. Somewhere in the distance, a dog begins to howl, then abruptly stops.

You wait for it to start again.

It does not.

Eventually, you close your eyes. The village sleeps beyond your walls, each household tucked into its own small world of warmth, worry, and familiar dreams.

Tomorrow will come.

For now, that is enough.

The temple emerges from the mist like the skeleton of something too ancient to die.

You reach it shortly before midnight, following a narrow path that winds between twisted trees and slabs of pale stone. The structure stands in a hollow beneath the high crag, its roof long since collapsed and its outer walls swallowed by ivy. Silver carvings cover the remaining pillars, catching the moonlight in thin, cold lines. Beyond the broken entrance, the darkness seems unusually deep, as though the shadows have gathered here and chosen not to leave.

Balor pauses at the threshold.

For the first time since you fled Highspire, he appears reluctant to enter.

You glance at him. “I thought you knew these woods.”

“I do.”

“And this place?”

His jaw tightens. “I know enough.”

It is not an answer, but you have begun to suspect that most of his answers are carefully measured portions of a much larger truth.

You step inside.

The air changes immediately. The metallic taste that has followed you through the forest sharpens, mingling with the scent of wet stone and something faintly sweet, like flowers pressed between the pages of an old book. Your boots disturb a thin layer of silver-grey dust. Broken tiles lie scattered across the floor, their surfaces marked with the same intricate patterns carved into the standing stones outside.

The temple must once have been magnificent. Pillars rise along either side of the central hall, each carved with twisting branches, crescent shapes, and mirrored figures whose faces have been worn smooth by time. At the far end stands an altar of pale stone, split down the middle by a jagged crack. Behind it, the remains of a circular arch frame the misty forest beyond.

There are no statues of gods. No offerings. No signs of worship that you recognise.

Instead, every carving seems to turn towards the altar.

You look back at Balor.

He has remained near the entrance, arms crossed, his expression carefully blank. The broken silver rings around his wrists catch the moonlight, their etched symbols almost identical to those covering the pillars. He stares into the mist beyond the doorway as though the temple holds nothing worth examining.

Yet his fingers have curled tightly against his sleeves.

“You can come inside,” you say. “The stones won't bite.”

“An observation based on extensive experience?”

“An observation based on the fact that you are standing in the doorway looking as though you'd rather face Marek's entire patrol.”

That earns you a brief, humourless smile.

“I have faced worse than Marek.”

“I'm sure you have.”

You move farther into the hall, studying the carvings. Their precision fascinates you. Every line is repeated on the opposite side of the pillar, reflected so perfectly that the pattern appears to continue into itself. In places, the silver inlay has darkened. In others, it remains bright, untouched by centuries of weather.

You recognise the symbols around Balor's wrists among them.

The sight sends a small, uneasy thrill through you. The rings were not simply restraints made by the Bone Coven. Their design belongs to something older, something that existed before the village, before the garrison, perhaps before the kingdoms that now claim these woods.

“Balor.”

He does not turn.

“What are these markings?”

“Old script.”

“Can you read it?”

“Yes.”

“And?”

“And I am not going to translate every inscription you find interesting.”

You give him a flat look. “You are remarkably good at making yourself difficult to help.”

“I have survived this long without your help.”

“Have you? Because from where I'm standing, you look as though your own wrists are slowly cutting you apart.”

His gaze snaps to yours.

For a moment, the air between you tightens. You have touched something he did not intend to expose, and the silence that follows is more revealing than any answer could have been.

Then he looks away.

“Leave the altar alone,” he says.

Naturally, you look at it.

The central stone is smooth except for the deep crack running through its middle. Mirrored carvings spiral outwards from a small depression at its centre, their lines converging around a symbol you recognise from the silver rings. The pattern resembles two interlocking circles, one whole and one broken.

You approach slowly.

The closer you get, the warmer your skin becomes. The pressure beneath your collarbone returns, gathering into a steady pulse that seems to answer the altar's silent presence. You raise your hand, intending only to trace the edge of the carving.

Your fingertips touch the stone.

White light erupts through the temple.

The pillars flare simultaneously, their silver lines blazing so brightly that the entire hall becomes a field of reflected brilliance. The floor vibrates beneath your feet. Somewhere above, loose stones tumble from the broken arch, striking the ground with sharp cracks.

You jerk backwards, but before you can pull away, Balor crosses the hall in a fraction of a second.

His hand closes around your wrist.

The grip is crushingly firm, his fingers locking just above your pulse as he tears your hand away from the altar. The light vanishes almost as quickly as it appeared, leaving the temple in darkness except for the moonlight filtering through the broken roof.

You stumble against him.

His other hand catches your waist before you can fall. For one suspended moment, you are pressed against his chest, your wrist trapped in his grasp and your free hand braced against the front of his coat.

He is breathing hard.

So are you.

His face is close enough for you to see the fine lines of exhaustion around his eyes, the silver scars disappearing beneath his collar, and the faint glow that still moves beneath his skin. His expression is no longer detached. Fear, anger, and something far more difficult to name have broken through his composure.

“Are you trying to get yourself killed?” he demands.

“You told me to leave it alone. You didn't say touching it would set the entire temple on fire.”

“It didn't set the temple on fire.”

“An important distinction.”

His eyes narrow, but his hand remains around your wrist.

You feel his thumb resting against your pulse point. Beneath his touch, your heartbeat seems impossibly loud. The warmth under your collarbone has spread through your chest, and you become acutely aware of the closeness between you: the solid line of his body, the warmth of his breath against your cheek, the tension in his arm as he holds you steady.

He looks down at where your skin meets his.

Something flickers across his face.

His grip loosens, though he does not release you immediately.

“You should not be able to wake this place,” he says quietly.

“Why?”

“Because it was built to recognise those who made the bindings. Not those trapped inside them.”

His words settle between you.

You glance at the altar. The mirrored carvings have gone dark, but a single silver line remains illuminated in the central crack. It pulses once, in time with your heartbeat.

Balor follows your gaze. His expression closes again, the brief vulnerability disappearing behind familiar coldness. Yet his fingers linger at your wrist for one moment longer before he finally lets go.

You could ask about the ritual that bound him here, forcing him to confront the history he is so determined to conceal. Or you could challenge the distance he has rebuilt between you, making him admit that your touch affected him as much as the altar did.

text.content:
Night settles over the wild without ever becoming entirely dark.

The trees stand in close ranks around your camp, their branches interlocking overhead until the moon appears only in fragments between the leaves. Mist drifts through the hollows, silver at its edges, and the distant sounds of the forest seem strangely muted. Even the stream below the shrine has fallen quiet, its earlier rush reduced to a soft murmur beneath the roots.

You sit beside a small, smokeless fire that burns with a pale amber glow.

Balor refuses to sit.

He paces the perimeter of the camp with the restless precision of a caged animal, checking the dark between the trees, pausing to listen, then moving again. The broken silver rings at his wrists catch the firelight whenever he turns. Occasionally, his fingers close around one of them, and a faint line of light travels beneath his skin before vanishing into his sleeve.

You have stopped asking him whether he is tired.

The first time you did, he looked at you as though you had asked whether stone becomes weary of being a mountain. Fae of his standing, he explained, have little use for mortal sleep.

You suspect that was not the whole truth.

There are many things Balor tells you with absolute confidence. There are just as many he avoids telling you at all.

You pull your cloak more tightly around your shoulders and stare into the flames.

He caught me before I fell.

The thought arrives uninvited.

You immediately try to dismiss it. Anyone standing close enough would have caught you. You had been about to stumble, the temple had been shaking, and Balor had reacted quickly. There is nothing remarkable about that.

Except that he crossed the entire hall before you had time to draw breath.

Except that his hand remained at your waist after you had regained your balance.

Except that, for one brief moment, he had looked at you as though the possibility of your being hurt was something he could not tolerate.

You shift uncomfortably.

He needs me alive.

That explanation is considerably more sensible. He has called you a key more than once. Whatever lies beneath the forest, whatever the ancient bindings conceal, your blood appears to matter to him. Perhaps he fears losing the only means he has of achieving whatever he has planned.

You glance at his wrists.

The rings are not decorative. Their edges have broken his skin, and the silver light beneath the metal seems to pulse with a rhythm of its own. You remember the way the altar answered your touch, and the sudden change in his expression when he realised what had happened.

He knows more about you than he is willing to admit.

But does he know what he intends to do with you?

That question troubles you more than the others.

Balor pauses at the edge of the clearing. His head turns slightly, and you have the uncomfortable impression that he has heard every thought passing through your mind.

Ridiculous. You cannot possibly know that.

Then his gaze settles on you.

You look down at the fire a moment too late.

Wonderful, Elara. You've survived a village burning, escaped an armed patrol, and discovered that your blood can wake ancient magic. Now you're embarrassed because a dangerous Fae man caught you looking at him.

You press your lips together.

There is something deeply unfair about his appearance. Even exhausted, even with blood drying beneath the broken rings, he carries himself with a composure that makes the surrounding forest seem less certain of its own existence. His dark coat is torn at one shoulder. His hair falls untidily across his forehead, and a narrow scar cuts through one eyebrow. He looks less like the terrifying figure who emerged from violet fire and more like someone who has spent too long surviving things he should never have had to endure.

You remind yourself that appearances are not evidence of character.

You remind yourself that he threatened you in the village square.

You remind yourself that he has repeatedly referred to you as a key.

All of these things remain true.

Unfortunately, so does the memory of his hand around your wrist, the startling warmth of his body against yours, and the way his voice had changed when he asked whether you were trying to get yourself killed.

You look back at the fire.

This is not attraction. It is adrenaline. Exhaustion. The natural response to being thrown into a dangerous situation with someone who might be the difference between life and death.

The explanation sounds convincing.

It also sounds suspiciously like something you are telling yourself because the alternative is inconvenient.

A twig snaps beyond the clearing.

Balor moves instantly. One moment he is standing beside a tree; the next, he is between you and the sound, one hand raised as silver light gathers along his fingers.

You stop breathing.

Nothing emerges from the darkness.

After several seconds, a small animal scurries through the undergrowth and disappears between the roots. Balor watches until it is gone, then lowers his hand.

“You can relax,” he says without looking at you.

“I was relaxed.”

He turns his head.

“You were gripping that stick as though you intended to challenge the entire forest with it.”

You look down. A half-burned branch lies clenched in your fist.

You place it beside the fire with as much dignity as possible.

“I prefer to be prepared.”

“So I have noticed.”

There is a trace of amusement in his voice. It catches you off guard, and you nearly smile before remembering that you are not supposed to find him amusing.

He notices that, too.

His expression changes—not into a smile, exactly, but into something quieter. For a few seconds, he simply watches you.

You expect him to make another remark. Instead, he returns to his slow circuit of the clearing.

That is somehow worse.

You find yourself wondering what he sees when he looks at you. Does he see the bloodline that can awaken ancient shrines? The mortal who might help him escape his bindings? Or does he occasionally forget, as you sometimes forget, that your meeting began with fire and violence?

Perhaps the question is meaningless. Balor has lived through centuries, if the old stories are even remotely true. You are a woman from a village that no longer exists. Whatever he feels, if he feels anything at all, it cannot carry the same weight for him that it might for you.

And yet he keeps looking back.

Once, when you raise your eyes, he is already watching you through the thin veil of heat rising from the fire. He does not look away when you meet his gaze. His expression is unreadable, but there is no mockery in it, no impatient calculation.

Only a quiet, complicated intensity that makes your chest tighten.

You hold his gaze for a moment longer than is comfortable.

Then you wonder whether he is testing you, measuring your willingness to challenge him, or simply waiting for you to make the first mistake.

Do not mistake attention for affection, you tell yourself. And do not mistake a moment of tenderness for trust.

The words settle you, though they do not entirely silence the questions.

The fire gives a soft crackle. Far away, something answers with a low, resonant hum. You feel it beneath your feet before you hear it properly, a vibration travelling through the ground from somewhere deep within the forest.

Balor's expression hardens.

He turns towards the sound, and the silver rings around his wrists begin to glow.

“What is that?” you ask.

“The leyline.”

You wait for him to explain.

He looks at you over his shoulder. “You will need to learn to recognise it. Your blood has already begun answering.”

“And you intend to teach me?”

“I intend to keep you alive.”

“That wasn't what I asked.”

“No,” he says quietly. “It wasn't.”

For a moment, neither of you speaks.

You watch him standing at the edge of the firelight, caught between the warmth of the camp and the darkness beyond it. You cannot decide whether he is protecting you because he needs you, because he feels responsible for what happened, or because some part of him has begun to care.

Perhaps he cannot decide either.

The thought is dangerous enough that you push it away.

The leyline hums again, stronger this time. Balor turns fully towards you, and the faint silver light beneath his skin illuminates the scars along his throat.

“Come morning,” he says, “I will show you how to listen without letting it answer through you.”

You should refuse. You should demand more information before agreeing to let him teach you anything involving your blood. You should remember that every secret he reveals seems to uncover three more.

Instead, you find yourself nodding.

The decision unsettles you almost as much as the magic.

As Balor resumes his watch, you settle beside the fire and draw your cloak around yourself. You will not trust him blindly. You will not surrender your judgement simply because he looks at you in a way you cannot explain.

But when you feel his gaze return to you across the flames, you do not immediately look away.

Let him wonder what I'm thinking for once.

The fire burns steadily between you, and the forest waits beyond its circle of light.

choices.text: Hold his gaze across the fire without blinking, testing his defences.
Look away into the dark, keeping your emotional distance from him.

text.content:
The ravine is colder than it looked from above.

Mist clings to the steep banks, gathering between exposed roots and drifting across the stream in pale ribbons. The rocks are slick with moss, and every few steps the ground disappears beneath a tangle of ferns or a curtain of hanging ivy. Somewhere ahead, water trickles over stone. Behind you, the ruined shrine has vanished into the darkness, leaving only the occasional silver glimmer through the trees.

Balor moves as though the terrain presents no difficulty whatsoever.

You, meanwhile, are beginning to reconsider the wisdom of following a man who appears to have no interest in whether you survive the journey.

“We need food,” you remind him as he steps over a fallen branch without breaking stride. “And water. Unless Fae of your standing can survive indefinitely on arrogance.”

He glances back.

“Arrogance is remarkably sustaining.”

“Then you must be exceptionally well nourished.”

A faint curve touches his mouth before disappearing. It is so brief that you almost convince yourself you imagined it.

Almost.

He points towards a patch of broad-leaved plants growing beside the stream. “Those berries are edible. The roots of the plant beside them can be boiled. The water is safe above the next bend, where the spring enters the ravine.”

“You could have told me that before we started climbing down.”

“You could have asked.”

“I did ask whether you knew these woods.”

“And I answered.”

“You said you knew them. You didn't mention that you intended to conduct a survival exercise.”

Balor crouches beside the plants and examines a cluster of dark berries. “If you would prefer to return to the village, I can arrange for Marek to meet you halfway.”

You fall silent.

The name has the desired effect. The image of the Wardens advancing through the burning square returns with unpleasant clarity: iron staffs, black armour, and the cold certainty with which Marek declared that you were coming into Coven custody. You remember the way they spoke about your blood as though it were a possession that had been misplaced.

No. You have no intention of returning to them.

Balor seems to understand that he has won the argument. He gathers several berries and places them in a small cloth pouch at his belt.

You kneel beside the stream, filling a spare flask. The water is bitterly cold against your fingers. When you glance up, you find him watching you.

“What?” you ask.

“Nothing.”

“You have been looking at me for the past several minutes.”

“I was wondering whether you always talk this much when frightened.”

You tighten the flask's stopper. “I was wondering whether you always mistake silence for intelligence.”

This time, his smile lasts a little longer.

It changes his face in a way you find inconvenient. The severity around his mouth eases, and for an instant he looks younger—or perhaps simply less burdened by whatever history he carries. The expression makes him seem almost approachable.

Then he looks away, and the moment closes.

You turn back to the stream.

There it is again.

That inexplicable shift in your attention whenever he lets some small piece of himself escape. You have known him for barely a handful of hours, and most of those hours have involved fleeing danger. He has threatened you, insulted you, and made it abundantly clear that he considers your blood more useful than your opinions.

You have excellent reasons not to like him.

So why do you keep looking for signs that there is something beneath his cold exterior?

Because you want to know whether you are safe, you tell yourself. Not because you care what he thinks of you.

It is a sensible explanation. You hold on to it.

Once you have collected enough food, Balor leads you farther along the stream towards a narrow shelf of rock. The path becomes treacherous, sloping sharply towards the water. He crosses first, placing each foot with effortless precision.

You follow, testing the stones before trusting your weight to them.

The next boulder is broad and covered in thick green moss. You step onto it carefully, one hand reaching for a low branch.

Your boot slips.

For one awful instant, the world tilts. The stream rushes beneath you, and the far bank seems to slide away. You reach for the branch, but your fingers close on empty air.

Then Balor is there.

His hand catches your forearm before you can fall. He pulls you sharply towards him, his grip iron-steady through the fabric of your sleeve. Your free hand strikes his chest, and he braces himself against the boulder, absorbing the force of your weight without so much as shifting his footing.

You end up pressed against him, one boot still balanced precariously on the slick stone.

Neither of you moves.

His fingers are wrapped around your arm. Through your sleeve, you feel the heat of his hand, startlingly warm against the cold mist. His other arm is positioned behind you, holding you away from the drop. You can feel the tension in his body, the controlled strength required to keep you upright.

You become acutely aware of how close you are.

The silver light beneath his skin has brightened. It traces the scars at his wrist and flickers beneath the broken rings, responding to something you cannot see. At the same time, warmth gathers beneath your collarbone, answering his touch with a slow, unmistakable pulse.

You stare at him.

He looks down at you.

His eyes are no longer cold. For a fraction of a second, something unguarded passes through them—alarm, perhaps, or anger at the thought of what might have happened if he had been slower.

There is something else, too, but you cannot name it before he seems to recognise that you are looking.

His jaw tightens.

He releases you as abruptly as though your skin has scorched him.

“Watch where you're stepping,” he mutters, turning towards the far bank.

You catch the rock with your hand and regain your balance. “I was watching.”

“Clearly.”

“You caught me.”

“I noticed.”

“Then perhaps a simple thank you would be more appropriate than another insult.”

He stops.

For a moment, you think he will turn and deliver some cutting reply. Instead, he stands with his back to you, one hand curled into a fist at his side. The silver light around his wrist flickers once, then disappears beneath his sleeve.

“Do not make more of it than it was,” he says.

The words are quiet, almost flat.

You feel an unexpected sting of irritation.

I wasn't going to.

Except that you were. Perhaps not consciously, perhaps not in any way you would admit aloud, but some part of you had been trying to understand what that moment meant. His grip had been protective, his expression unguarded, and the heat of his hand had seemed to linger even after he let go.

Now he is determined to erase it.

You step onto the far bank, keeping a careful distance between you.

“Don't worry,” you say. “I understand. You rescued a mortal. You would hate for anyone to think you had developed a conscience.”

Balor turns his head.

His expression is composed again, but the muscles along his jaw remain taut.

“You know nothing about my conscience.”

“No. You have made a remarkable effort to ensure that.”

The words hang between you.

For several seconds, neither of you speaks. The stream continues its quiet passage beneath the mist, and droplets fall from the leaves overhead. You can hear your own heartbeat, still too quick from the near fall.

Balor's gaze drops briefly to your forearm, where his fingers had held you. When he looks back at your face, his expression has changed. The coldness remains, but it seems more deliberate now, something he has put on rather than something that comes naturally.

“Stay on the higher ground,” he says. “The mist conceals deeper pools beyond the next bend.”

It is not an apology.

It is, however, a warning offered without mockery.

You nod once and follow him along the bank. Neither of you mentions what happened again, but the silence between you feels different from before. You are aware of every time he glances back to check your position. He is aware, you suspect, of every time you notice.

You cannot tell whether he is trying to keep you alive because he needs your blood, because he feels responsible for you, or because the thought of losing you has become unexpectedly difficult to tolerate.

Perhaps all three are true.

You decide not to ask. Not yet.

The path ahead climbs towards a narrow shelf overlooking the ravine. Beyond it, the mist gathers in a deep hollow where faint violet light pulses beneath the earth. Balor pauses to study it, his face once again unreadable.

“We should reach shelter before the leyline strengthens,” he says.

You move to stand beside him, leaving just enough space that your shoulders do not touch.

“Then lead the way,” you reply. “I'll try not to fall into anything else.”

His eyes flick towards you.

“And I'll try not to save you.”

You almost smile.

“See that you do.”

He turns towards the path, and you follow, carrying the food and water between you. The forest remains dangerous, the Wardens are still hunting, and the secrets surrounding your blood have only grown more troubling.

Yet beneath those immediate concerns lies another uncertainty, quieter and harder to dismiss.

You are beginning to suspect that Balor's distance is not proof that he feels nothing.

It may be proof that he has something to lose.

choices.text: Quietly thank him, noting how quickly he tries to rebuild his walls.
Stand your ground and call out his sudden coldness.

text.content:
The first warning is a taste of metal.

It spreads across your tongue, sharp and bitter, followed by a pressure beneath your breastbone that makes you stumble. The mist around the ravine shivers. Every bead of water clinging to the moss catches a faint violet light, and the stones beneath your boots begin to hum.

You stop breathing.

The sound is everywhere now. Not merely beneath the earth, but inside it—threaded through the roots of trees, the bones of the hills, the very blood moving through your veins. It rises in overlapping notes, some so deep you feel them in your teeth, others thin enough to make your skull ache.

The collarbone that has burned since Highspire answers with sudden, vicious heat.

Light spills between your fingers.

You jerk your hands against your chest, but the glow only intensifies. Fine silver lines race across your wrists, branching beneath your skin like cracks in glass. Violet sparks leap from your knuckles and strike the ground. Where they touch, dead leaves curl into ash without flame.

“Balor.”

His name comes out as little more than a breath.

He turns. For once, there is no lazy amusement in his expression.

“Don't move.”

The command arrives too late. Another pulse tears through you, lifting the hair along your arms. Light flares from your palms, illuminating the ravine walls and the twisted trees above. Somewhere beyond the ridge, a night bird shrieks and falls silent.

You imagine the glow rising above the canopy, a beacon visible from every road and watchtower for miles. You imagine Marek Thorne looking up from his ledger, recognising exactly what has begun to burn.

Your blood is telling the world where you are.

You try to close your fists. The magic surges in protest, bright enough to cast your shadow across the stones.

“Stop fighting it,” Balor snaps.

“I don't know what it is!”

“You know perfectly well what it is. You simply don't know how to listen.”

He crosses the distance between you before you can answer. One moment he stands several paces away; the next, his hands close around yours.

His fingers are freezing.

The shock of that cold cuts through the feverish light, and you draw a startled breath. He turns your hands over and presses your palms flat against his chest, holding them there with a firmness that leaves no room for argument.

“Stop fighting the current,” he commands, his voice dangerously low. “Channel it into me.”

You stare at him.

Up close, the damage the bindings have done to him is harder to ignore. Faint silver scars thread the skin above his collar, disappearing beneath his dark clothing. The broken rings at his wrists glimmer faintly, their edges etched with symbols that seem to shift whenever you try to study them. His eyes burn red-gold in the scattered light, but beneath their familiar arrogance lies something watchful and strained.

His breath warms your brow.

The contrast between that warmth and his icy hands is bewildering. So is the fact that he has placed himself between you and the open ravine, his body blocking the worst of the light from the ridge above.

You could mistake it for protection.

You refuse to be that foolish.

He needs me alive. The thought arrives with such immediate certainty that you seize it like a handhold. I'm the key. He has said as much himself. Whatever happens to me matters because of what my blood can open.

It is a sensible explanation. It ought to settle the strange, treacherous flutter beneath your ribs.

It doesn't.

“Look at me,” Balor says.

You lift your gaze.

“Not at the light. Not at the stones. Me.”

The magic bucks against your skin. Your first instinct is to force it down, to clamp every part of yourself around the power until it cannot escape. You have spent your life learning how to manage what you possess: a steady hand, a patient eye, a stubborn refusal to be frightened by things that require doing. None of those instincts help now.

The current is not something you can hold.

It is something passing through you.

You draw a breath and try to feel its direction. The hum beneath the earth deepens. The silver lines on your wrists pulse in time with it, and the light trembles between your palms and Balor's chest.

“Good,” he murmurs. “Now let it move.”

“I am letting it move.”

“No. You're trying to decide where it may go. There is a difference.”

You would like to tell him precisely what he can do with his lessons. Instead, you concentrate on the cold beneath your hands and the steady pressure of his fingers around yours.

There is something beneath his skin that answers the leyline's call. Not a heartbeat—not quite—but a slow, ancient rhythm, like distant thunder travelling through stone. You feel it through your palms, and your magic turns towards it with sudden, startling recognition.

The current changes direction.

Silver light streams from your hands into his chest.

Balor stiffens.

A bright arc bridges your palms, his skin, and the broken rings at his wrists. For one impossible heartbeat, the ravine disappears beneath a wash of white light. You see shapes that cannot be there: immense silver doors, a circle of figures with their faces hidden, and chains stretching into darkness so vast that your mind refuses to measure it.

Then you feel pain.

Not yours alone.

Something ancient and furious recoils inside Balor, and the force of it slams through the connection. You glimpse a prison made of bone and ash, a sky without stars, and a pair of hands bound in silver. The images vanish before you can understand them, leaving behind a sensation of cold so profound that it seems to have swallowed centuries.

Balor's eyes widen.

The arrogant mask shatters completely. For a single heartbeat, he looks neither dangerous nor untouchable. He looks wounded in a way that has nothing to do with the silver scars on his skin.

And he is looking at you as though you have reached somewhere no living person should be able to touch.

The connection tightens.

Your breath catches. You become aware of everything at once: the cold stone beneath your boots, the warmth of his breath, the pressure of his fingers, the faint tremor running through his body. You can feel the effort he is making to contain whatever has answered through you.

You can also feel that he is afraid.

The realisation is so unexpected that you almost lose your concentration.

Balor tears his hands away.

The silver arc snaps out of existence. You stagger backwards, catching yourself against a tree, while the last sparks scatter across the damp ground and fade. The ravine falls dark again. Its hum recedes to a distant murmur, leaving your ears ringing.

For several seconds, neither of you speaks.

Balor stands rigidly before you, his hands curled at his sides. The silver rings at his wrists have stopped glowing, but the scars around them look darker than before. He stares at you with an expression you cannot read, then turns his face away.

“Don't do that again,” he says.

“You told me to.”

“I told you to channel the current. I did not tell you to reach into places you cannot understand.”

“You could have explained the difference.”

“And you could have listened.”

The sharpness of his reply ought to make you angry. It does, but anger is complicated by the memory of his expression when the connection formed. You have seen him sneer at danger, mock your questions, and treat fear as a weakness other people possess. You have never seen him look at you as though you have discovered something he desperately wanted to keep buried.

What did I touch?

The question presses against your thoughts. You could ask it aloud. You could demand to know what you saw, why the magic recognised him, and why he looked almost frightened when your blood answered his.

Instead, you watch him retreat behind the familiar coldness.

“You're shaking,” he says.

“So are you.”

His gaze snaps back to yours.

For a moment, you think he will deny it. Then his hands close more tightly, hiding the tremor in his fingers.

“It's the leyline,” he says. “The old currents are growing stronger. Whatever happened at Highspire has disturbed more than one seal.”

“That doesn't explain what happened between us.”

“No.” His voice drops. “It doesn't.”

The admission hangs between you, more revealing than any explanation would have been.

Above the ravine, a thin violet glow pulses through the mist. Once. Twice. On the third pulse, you hear a distant metallic clang from somewhere beyond the ridge.

Balor's expression hardens.

“They felt that,” he says.

“Who?”

“The people who have been looking for you.”

He steps towards you, then stops himself, leaving a careful space between your bodies. His eyes flick briefly to your hands, where faint silver lines still linger beneath the skin.

“From now on, when the leyline calls, you tell me before you try to answer it. Do you understand?”

You look at the distance he has deliberately placed between you. Part of you wants to close it, to discover whether the strange warmth of that connection remains. Another part remembers the images you saw and the pain that passed through him.

You are beginning to understand that Balor's secrets are not simply things he refuses to tell you. Some of them may be things he cannot bear to have known.

And that makes him more dangerous, not less.

The metallic clang sounds again, closer this time.

Balor turns towards the ridge. “We move. Now.”

He offers no hand, but he waits until you are beside him before leading you into the mist.

You follow, your palms still tingling with the memory of his skin, and wonder whether the connection was merely a lesson in controlling your power—or the first sign that your blood recognises something in him that your mind has not yet understood.

choices.text: Let the experience soften your guard, accepting his guidance.
Push back against his abrupt withdrawal, asserting your own power.

text.content:
The mist parts at the edge of the gorge, revealing a narrow stone bridge.

It spans a deep cleft in the earth, its ancient arch slick with rain and green with moss. Far below, unseen water roars through the darkness. The path on the opposite side winds between black pines, disappearing into the wild country beyond. It should be a straightforward crossing.

Balor stops so abruptly that you nearly collide with him.

“What is it?” you ask.

He doesn't answer. His gaze travels over the bridge, the cliff edges, and the mist beyond. The silver rings around his wrists have begun to glow faintly, casting thin lines of light across his fingers.

Then you see the figure standing at the far end of the bridge.

Marek Thorne.

The First Scholar of Ash and Bone looks exactly as he did in the burning square of Highspire: composed, immaculate, and entirely untouched by the chaos around him. His dark coat is replaced by a long cloak threaded with cold iron, its heavy hem dragging across the wet stones. In one hand, he carries a binding staff crowned with interlocking metal rings. In the other, he holds a narrow blade whose silver-steel edge catches the pale light.

Behind him, a hunting squad emerges from the mist.

Eight Wardens, perhaps more. Their armour is reinforced with bone charms, their faces hidden behind iron-mesh masks. Each carries a length of heavy chain, blackened by age and etched with runes that make your skin prickle even from a distance.

Marek regards Balor with the detached interest of a scholar examining a specimen.

“Balor,” he says. “You have made yourself remarkably difficult to retrieve.”

Balor's expression hardens.

“Thorne. I see the Coven still sends its least imaginative men to do its dirtiest work.”

“You mistake efficiency for a lack of imagination.”

Marek raises the binding staff.

The Wardens move.

“Run,” Balor says.

You don't have time to decide whether to obey. Chains fly through the mist, their heavy links turning in the air. One catches Balor across the chest. Another coils around his left arm, and a third snaps around his ankle before he can retreat.

The runes flare.

Balor's silver light erupts in a blinding burst, then collapses as though something has crushed it between invisible hands. He staggers, teeth bared, while the chains tighten. Smoke rises where the cold iron touches his skin.

You have never seen him so quickly subdued.

He twists violently, trying to break the links through sheer force, but the Wardens have trained for this exact moment. Two pull from behind while another drives a hooked length of chain around his shoulder. Their movements are coordinated, relentless, and merciless.

Marek advances without hurry.

“You are a remnant of a failed war,” he says. “The fact that you have remained alive is a historical inconvenience, not a claim to freedom.”

Balor laughs once, a harsh sound without humour.

“And yet you brought an entire squad to collect me.”

“I brought an entire squad to ensure that you cannot escape.”

Marek draws the silver-steel blade across the binding staff. The metal sings, a thin, unpleasant note that sets your teeth on edge. Balor recoils as the sound passes through him. His knees bend under the pressure, and the chains pull him down towards the stones.

Something cold settles in your stomach.

They know exactly how to hurt him.

Marek turns his grey eyes towards you.

“And there is our missing key.”

The Wardens shift their formation. Two break away from Balor and approach you, chains ready in their hands.

“You will come with us,” Marek says. “You have demonstrated an unfortunate tendency to interfere with matters you do not understand. I intend to correct that.”

You glance at Balor.

His gaze catches yours through the chains. The fury in his expression is unmistakable, but beneath it lies a warning so sharp that you almost feel it physically.

Don't let them take you.

The thought may be yours. It may be something left over from the leyline connection. You cannot tell.

You remember the current moving through your hands, the way the stones answered when you stopped fighting the magic. You remember Balor telling you to listen rather than command.

The first Warden lunges.

You move before fear can stop you.

You turn your attention towards the bridge. Beneath the wet stone, the leyline hums, ancient and immense. You feel it threading through the gorge walls, through the roots of the pines, through the bones of the hills. The current presses against your palms, waiting.

You do not try to seize it.

You listen.

Then you release it.

The kinetic wave erupts from your body with enough force to make the bridge shudder. The approaching Wardens are thrown backwards. Their chains fly from their hands, clattering against the stone. The binding staff's runes flash, and three of the carved wooden shafts carried by the squad splinter in the shock.

The line breaks.

For a heartbeat, the only sound is the roar of water below.

You stare at your hands. Silver light winds between your fingers, fading into the mist.

You did not mean to unleash so much power.

But you did it.

Balor looks at you with an expression you cannot interpret. Surprise flashes across his face, quickly followed by something fiercer.

“Now would be an excellent time to keep doing that,” he says.

Marek's composure finally cracks.

“Take them both!”

The Wardens surge forward.

Balor tears one arm free, dragging a broken chain behind him. He moves like a blade released from its sheath, striking with brutal precision. Silver light flashes from his hand and throws one Warden against the bridge's stone parapet. Another tries to close around his legs, but Balor catches the chain and sends its owner sprawling.

You turn towards the nearest attacker. His staff sweeps towards your head. You duck beneath it and push outwards with both palms, sending a sharp pulse through the stones. The Warden loses his footing and crashes into his companion.

The two of you fall into a desperate rhythm.

Balor draws their attention while you disrupt their formation. You strike when they gather, releasing bursts of force that send weapons skidding across the bridge. He moves through the openings you create, his silver magic flashing between the Wardens before they can recover.

You are not fighting like a trained warrior. You have no elegant footwork, no knowledge of where to place a blade. You are simply trying to survive, listening for the current beneath the chaos and releasing it wherever you sense an opening.

Each surge makes your collarbone burn hotter.

The power is exhilarating in a way that frightens you. For the first time, you understand that the magic inside you is not merely a curse or a beacon for creatures who want to use you. It can answer when you call. It can change the course of a fight.

But it is not free.

Your fingers begin to tremble. The bridge seems to sway beneath your feet, and the mist brightens at its edges. You feel the leyline pulling at you, eager for another release, and force yourself to breathe rather than surrender to it.

Across the bridge, Marek watches you.

He has not joined the struggle. He stands beyond the broken formation, his binding staff planted against the stones, studying each movement as though your power is an experiment unfolding precisely as he expected.

That is more frightening than his anger.

“You see?” he calls to you. “You have no control. Every use makes you more visible to the things buried beneath this world.”

“Then perhaps you should stop trying to bury people beneath it,” you shout back.

Marek's expression goes still.

He moves.

One instant he stands at the far end of the bridge. The next, he is inside Balor's guard, his silver-steel blade cutting a bright line through the mist. Balor twists aside, but the binding chains still drag at his limbs. He cannot move quickly enough to avoid the strike entirely.

Marek's blade slices across his shoulder.

Balor snarls and drives a burst of silver fire into Marek's chest. The Scholar staggers backwards, boots scraping against wet stone, but he does not fall. His binding staff strikes the bridge, and the chains around Balor flare again.

Balor drops to one knee.

You feel the change in the leyline before you understand what has happened. The current beneath the bridge surges towards him, then recoils as the cold iron suppresses his magic. The pressure in your chest grows unbearable.

You could unleash another wave.

You could break the remaining chains, perhaps. You might even throw Marek from the bridge.

But your hands shake, and the current is becoming harder to distinguish from the wild, hungry pulse of your own blood.

Marek sees your hesitation.

He turns the blade in his hand and steps towards Balor's exposed flank.

“Your usefulness has been noted,” he tells you. “Your cooperation is no longer necessary.”

Balor looks up.

For the first time, you see him calculate the distance between you, Marek, and the broken section of the bridge. His gaze flicks towards the forest beyond the gorge. A desperate possibility passes between you without words.

The bridge is old. Its central arch is cracked where your first kinetic wave struck. Another concentrated surge might bring part of it down, separating Marek and his Wardens from the forest path.

But someone must create the opening.

Marek raises his blade.

You move.

Everything narrows to a single instant: the silver-steel edge, Balor's blood on his torn sleeve, the faint glow of your own hands. You know what the next heartbeat may cost. You know that either choice will change what exists between you and the dangerous, infuriating Fae who has led you through the wild.

There is no time to ask him what he wants.

There is only time to decide.

choices.text: Throw yourself in front of Marek's blade to let Balor escape into the woods.
Let Balor shield you from the blow, taking a severe cold-iron strike to his side.

text.content:
You do not remember deciding to save him.

You remember the weight of Balor against your shoulder, the dark blood slipping between your fingers, and the terrible cold spreading from the wound in his side. You remember the bridge disappearing behind a curtain of mist as you dragged him towards the trees. After that, everything becomes a sequence of desperate choices: a narrow deer track, a steep descent, the roar of water growing louder, and Balor's increasingly unsteady insistence that he can walk without your help.

He makes it almost to the waterfall.

Then his knees give way.

You catch him beneath the arms, but his weight forces you both against the damp rock. For a moment, he hangs there, breathing through clenched teeth, his head bowed close to yours.

“Let go,” he mutters.

“No.”

“Elara.”

It is the first time he has said your name like that—not as a warning, a taunt, or a calculation. It sounds like an appeal he resents having to make.

You tighten your grip.

“You can argue with me when you're not about to collapse.”

His laugh is a faint, broken sound.

“Bossy little mortal.”

“Bleeding, arrogant Fae.”

“An unfortunate combination.”

“Then stop talking and keep moving.”

You half-drag him behind the waterfall.

The opening is almost invisible from the outside, concealed by the white rush of water and the overhanging roots of an ancient tree. Beyond it, a narrow passage opens into a shallow cave. Ash coats the floor in a fine grey layer, stirred into small spirals by the wind slipping through cracks in the stone. The air is cold, but the waterfall muffles the world beyond, turning the sounds of the forest into a distant, constant rumble.

You lower Balor against the wall.

He tries to straighten immediately. One hand braces against the stone; the other clamps over his side. His fingers are trembling.

“Don't,” you say.

“I wasn't—”

“You were about to stand up.”

“I was considering it.”

“You can consider it sitting down.”

His eyes lift to yours. Even now, pale with pain, he manages to look offended.

You almost smile. The impulse surprises you. There is something absurd about finding him irritatingly familiar at the very moment he is coming apart before you.

Then he shifts, and a dark stain spreads beneath his hand.

The smile disappears.

“Let me see.”

“No.”

The answer is immediate, automatic. He turns his body away, trying to hide the wound as though secrecy might make it less severe.

You stare at him.

“Balor, the blade was cold iron. I saw what it did to you on the bridge. If the poison is spreading, you cannot simply glare it into submission.”

“I have survived considerably worse.”

“That isn't an argument.”

“It is a statement of experience.”

“And your experience appears to be that you survive things by refusing to let anyone help you.”

He looks at you sharply.

For a moment, you think he will order you out of the cave. Instead, his gaze drops to his bloodied hand.

“Usually,” he says quietly, “there is no one left to help.”

The words settle between you.

You have heard him speak of prisons, bindings, and wars as though they were distant inconveniences. You have seen the silver scars on his wrists, but he has always carried them like a challenge. You have never considered what it might mean to live so long that everyone who once knew you has become a memory, or that every person who approaches might be a hunter, a jailer, or someone hoping to use your power.

You kneel in front of him.

“I'm here.”

The simplicity of it makes you feel exposed. You could have said that you needed him alive, that he was your only guide through the wild, that you could not afford to lose the one person who understood what your blood was becoming.

All of those things are true.

None is what you mean.

Balor studies you, searching for the condition attached to the offer. You can almost see him looking for the hidden bargain, the debt, the weakness he might later have to repay.

Whatever he finds in your expression makes his own change.

“That's a dangerous thing to promise,” he says.

“I didn't promise anything. I said I'm here.”

His gaze falls away.

“Then make yourself useful.”

The old sharpness has returned to his voice, but it no longer convinces either of you.

You find a small knife in your pack and tear a strip from the cleanest part of your spare shirt. The water has soaked through your sleeves, and your fingers are stiff with cold. You work carefully, trying not to look at the amount of blood on your hands.

His coat is charred along the side, the fabric fused to the wound in places. You explain what you need to do before cutting it away. Balor gives a short nod, jaw tight, and looks towards the cave entrance.

The first cut draws a sharp breath from him.

“I'm sorry,” you say.

“Don't apologise for doing what must be done.”

“Would you prefer I apologise for the state of your coat?”

“It's an excellent coat.”

You glance at the ruined fabric.

“It was.”

His mouth moves faintly. Almost a smile, though pain quickly erases it.

You work the cloth free, exposing the wound beneath his ribs. The cut is deep, its edges darkened by the cold iron's poison. Fine silver threads flicker beneath his skin, struggling to close the damage before the darkness can spread. The ancient rings embedded around his wrists glow weakly, answering the poison with a pulse that seems to travel through his entire body.

You have never seen them this clearly.

They are not merely jewellery, nor even restraints fastened around him. Their silver edges disappear beneath his skin, woven into the scars as though the metal has become part of his body. Tiny symbols cover their surfaces. Some are familiar from the ruined shrine; others seem to shift when the light catches them.

Your collarbone warms in response.

Balor notices.

“Don't touch the rings.”

“I wasn't going to.”

“You were thinking about it.”

“You don't know what I'm thinking.”

His eyes meet yours.

“Don't I?”

The question is quiet enough to unsettle you.

You turn back to the wound, but the words follow you. The leyline connection has left you with an uncomfortable awareness of him—not a voice in your mind, not a way to read his thoughts, but a memory of his presence beneath the surface of his composure. You remember the fear you felt when the current passed between you, and the shock of discovering that the untouchable creature before you could be frightened at all.

You wonder what he remembers of you.

Perhaps the power. Perhaps the key.

Perhaps nothing else.

As you reach to lift the torn fabric away from the wound, your fingers brush the scarred skin above his ribs.

Balor catches your wrist.

You freeze.

His grip is weak, but immediate. His hand closes around you as though instinct has moved before thought. You expect him to push you away, to retreat behind a cutting remark, or to tell you that you have crossed some boundary he has never bothered to explain.

He does none of those things.

He simply holds on.

His eyes are fixed on your face. Without the usual arrogance, they look older than you can comprehend. Not in appearance, but in the weight behind them. The red-gold has dimmed, leaving a tired, almost human uncertainty that he seems unable to conceal.

You could pull away.

You don't.

“What is it?” you ask.

His thumb shifts once against your wrist. His fingers tighten, then loosen, as though he has only just realised what he is doing.

“I don't know.”

It is the most honest answer he has ever given you.

You lower your voice. “Does it hurt?”

“Yes.”

The admission seems to cost him more than the word should.

“Then hold on if it helps.”

His expression changes.

You have not offered him comfort in any grand or noble form. You have not promised to free him, save him, or undo centuries of suffering. You have simply given him permission not to pretend for a moment.

He looks down at your wrist.

“I was not always like this,” he says eventually.

You wait.

“I know that sounds ridiculous. Everyone changes. Everyone becomes something they weren't.” His gaze shifts towards the waterfall, beyond which the world is still hunting him. “But I remember a time when I could enter a room without calculating every exit. When I could hear someone laugh without wondering what they wanted. When a hand reaching towards me did not make me think of chains.”

The last word is barely audible.

Your throat tightens.

You think of Highspire, of your cottage and the familiar warmth of the hearth, of Kael's voice and the ordinary life that seemed too small until it was taken from you. You have been so busy fearing what you might become that you have barely allowed yourself to grieve what you have already lost.

“I keep thinking about home,” you say.

Balor looks back at you.

“I know I can't go back. Not to the way it was. But I keep remembering stupid things. The sound of the door when someone came in. The smell of bread. The way the roof creaked when the wind changed.” You swallow. “I thought I wanted something extraordinary to happen to me once. Something that would make my life mean more than it did. Now I would give anything to have one ordinary evening back.”

The words leave you before you can stop them.

You look down, embarrassed by their simplicity. You have spent your life being useful, keeping your worries manageable, telling yourself that tomorrow will provide whatever today lacks. Yet here, in a cave behind a waterfall, you find yourself admitting how badly you want something you cannot have.

Balor does not make a joke.

He does not tell you that ordinary life is an illusion, or that you should be grateful to have survived. He watches you with a stillness that feels different from his usual scrutiny.

“I remember the first house I ever entered,” he says. “It stood beside a river that no longer exists. There were blue flowers in the windows and a crooked table in the kitchen. The woman who lived there insisted I was too thin and fed me until I could barely move.”

You blink.

“You had a house?”

“I had many places I called home.”

The past tense is deliberate.

“What happened to them?”

“The world happened.”

He looks away, and you understand that this is as much as he can offer tonight.

After a moment, his hand loosens around your wrist. He seems about to withdraw it, but you turn your palm slightly, giving him the choice to remain without making him ask.

He takes it.

The gesture is small. There is no promise in it, no declaration, no sudden certainty that you can trust one another. Yet something shifts between you. For once, neither of you is trying to win.

You clean the wound as carefully as you can, using the water gathered in your flask and the clean strips of cloth. Balor endures the pain in silence, his hand resting loosely around yours whenever you pause. His breathing remains uneven, and the poison has not stopped spreading, but the worst of the bleeding slows.

When you finish binding his side, you settle against the opposite wall, close enough to watch him but leaving him room to move.

“Will you survive?” you ask.

He considers the question.

“Yes,” he says. Then, after a pause, “I think so.”

It is not the answer you wanted, but you recognise the effort it takes him to give it honestly.

Outside, the waterfall continues its endless rush. The cave smells of wet stone, ash, and blood. Your hands are stained, your body exhausted, and the power beneath your skin has settled into a low, persistent hum.

Balor's eyes begin to close.

Just before sleep claims him, he speaks again.

“Elara?”

“Yes?”

“If the Coven finds us, you must leave me.”

You look at the man who has spent the night teaching you to listen to a power neither of you understands, who has just trusted you with memories he has likely kept buried for centuries.

“No,” you say.

His eyes open.

“You haven't heard the rest.”

“I heard enough.”

For a long moment, he studies you. Then the faintest trace of his familiar, infuriating expression returns.

“You are going to be a terrible student.”

“Then you'll have to keep teaching me.”

He almost smiles.

This time, when his eyes close, he does not let go of your hand.

And you remain beside him, listening to the water and the distant hum of the leyline, understanding that vulnerability is not the same as trust. It is merely the moment when someone allows you to see what they have spent their life hiding.

What you choose to do with that knowledge is still yours to decide.

choices.text: Stay by his side through the night, holding his hand as he heals.
Carefully examine his silver binding rings while he sleeps, plotting how to master him.
Focus on unspooling the land's curse, knowing you must eventually set him free.
